# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-09 22:56 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 90 active entries of tips_notebook.json (6 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier versions are in history/.

## Everyone
- Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads. Accusing someone and then voting No or Innocent on them is exactly the mismatch Vigilantes shoot and the Village should scan for. (seen in 2 games)
- A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment. A Lookout on the Katana holder sees nothing of the holder's attack, and killing an attacker at night doesn't cancel their attack that night. (seen in 3 games)
- Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction. Actions are optional, most roles aren't unique, and you must recheck who sent each PM and the exact wording of results; one reversed fact can discredit a true claimant. (seen in 2 games)
- Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions, unless a Clerk may hold an unused rig. Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case. (seen in 3 games)
- Fortune Teller numbers are unordered, and one visitor can cover two targets (e.g. a Katana holder using their own action). List every way a count could fit before using it, and never hang on a count alone.

## Village
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer. (seen in 4 games)
- Two Sheriff claimants calling each other Evil can both be telling the truth, since Jesters and Executioners read Evil. Wait a day or find a mechanical check instead of hanging whoever sounded better. (seen in 2 games)
- Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them, and weigh these links above unverifiable late claims. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. Investigators never announce tonight's target, only resolved results. While a Ritualist may be alive, never name another living player's exact role. (seen in 5 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack, or who is role-blocked night after night, is likely real. Don't vote Guilty on an investigator just for having no results. (seen in 3 games)
- Keep a ledger of trial votes, announced totals, deaths and blocks. If a total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists: recompute the threshold, find the voter who matches every extra vote, and act before evil reaches half. (seen in 2 games)
- Ask everyone for a named suspect so you have a record, but a stack of echoed soft leans is not evidence. Watch for Yakuza nominating the pile-on target. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hang a power claimant just because the claim came late; ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits. (seen in 2 games)
- Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and surviving an attack with no Medic can mean innate Defense. (seen in 2 games)
- When a Clerk rig is announced, the nominator, the pushers and the Guilty voters are your prime suspects. Hang from that group next.

## Yakuza
- Do the vote math in night chat. If your Innocent votes (plus a doubled ballot) can save a teammate, defend them; if not, vote Guilty with the town, because lone No or Innocent votes on a flipped teammate become the case against you. (seen in 6 games)
- Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive and that tokens can be audited. Never claim something a living Lookout or Tracker can contradict, and don't have two members claim Vanilla. (seen in 4 games)
- Every member submits their action and Katana vote every night; confirm the holder and target in chat. With two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 3 games)
- After a failed attack, assume a protector or innate Defense: block or kill the Medic, or push the survivor to the gallows, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 3 games)
- Give the Katana to your least valuable member with no reason to visit. Never visit a suspected or claimed Veteran; hang them instead. (seen in 2 games)
- No Day 1 PMs between teammates, and give each teammate different wording; PM triangles and scripted lines become the town's lead for the whole game. (seen in 2 games)
- Parity doesn't end the game. At 2v2, vote No on every nomination, kill at night, then hang the last villager 2-1. (seen in 2 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged.

## Sheriff
- Post your target and result in your first speech after getting it, and keep your will current. A result held back and revealed after a counterclaim looks retrofitted.
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result on a suspected attacker clears nothing. Say so when you post it. (seen in 3 games)

## Medic
- Protect every night from N1: vocal analysts early, claimed investigators later. Free Standard Defense stops the Katana. (seen in 4 games)
- You get no feedback, so never claim a confirmed save. Say your protection is consistent with the target surviving. (seen in 2 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, a flipped Yakuza's vote or PM partners, votes contradicting reads), never on a behavioral read. Use Basic shots and never announce whom you'll shoot. (seen in 2 games)

## Veteran
- Alert on nights you drew attention, not quiet ones. Once you claim, Yakuza avoid you, so claim late and never reveal your remaining tokens.

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3 or more living players are doused or as soon as you're suspected. Ignite is Astral, but Strong Defense stops it.

## Executioner
- Fake-claim Sheriff early with an Evil result on your target and a simple reason. Leading first makes their counterclaim look reactionary.

A contradiction between two claims proves at least one account is false; it does not identify which claimant is evil. Before a guilty vote, compare both claimants' incentives and consider neutral roles, Roleplayer false results, and other mechanical explanations.

Use scarce shots on a mechanically grounded suspect, such as a meaningful claim conflict combined with other evidence—not on behavior alone. Match attack strength to the target's likely defense: a stronger-than-needed attack can waste tokens that might decide a later night.

tips_feedback.tip: Vigilante: Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, a flipped Yakuza's vote or PM partners, votes contradicting reads), never on a behavioral read. Use Basic shots and never announce whom you'll shoot.
tips_feedback.why: The Mallory shot was based on the conflicting Medic claims and the Alice visitor evidence, not merely behavior, and it killed the Yakuza Pharmacist. However, Strong spent all three tokens; a lower attack would likely have sufficed against her.

tips_feedback.tip: Yakuza: After a failed attack, assume a protector or innate Defense: block or kill the Medic, or push the survivor to the gallows, rather than retrying blindly.
tips_feedback.why: After the Katana attack on Alice failed, the Yakuza role-blocked Niaj on Night 2 and killed Grace. That prevented Niaj's protection from saving Grace.

tips_feedback.tip: Everyone: Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions. Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case.
tips_feedback.why: The Heidi trial had a real Lookout/Tracker contradiction, but treating that contradiction as enough to hang her failed to distinguish a Jester from an evil liar. Her revenge then killed Ivan. A contradiction is a reason to investigate, not necessarily a reason to execute.

lessons.tip: An Evil result is not the same as a Yakuza result. Check appearance exceptions: Ex-Con appears Evil, a Fabricator can frame someone for that night, and Serial Killer appears Not Evil to the Sheriff. State what the result proves—and what it doesn’t.

Keep direct observations, role claims, and deductions separate. A Lookout list can put a killer among a set of visitors, but it does not identify which visitor attacked; verify the timeline before calling later claims corroboration.

Don’t assume a role is unique unless its rules say so. Conversely, a duplicate claim is not proof that either claimant is lying; seek independent evidence such as revealed roles, token limits, or mechanically incompatible actions.

Treat claims and vote patterns as evidence, not confirmation. Roleplayers can receive plausible false investigative results, and Jesters benefit from being hanged, so an apparently bad result or a guilty vote needs context.

Share enough information to let others test your case, but be mindful that private-message contents are visible to recipients and message activity is public. Coordinate around specific claims and timelines rather than building a case from private-message volume.

lessons.tip: Directly counter-claiming a confirmed or credible investigative role with a fabricated mechanical result is one of the cleanest ways to secure a quick execution, especially if you double down and firmly reject town's attempt to excuse you as an innocent Roleplayer.

Track the chronology of claims versus information: when an investigative claimant names multiple visitors before any of those players speak or claim, that report is nearly impossible for evil to fake and should be treated as extremely credible.

When fake-claiming a token-limited role like Surveyor (2 tokens), never provide more reports than the role mechanically possesses; town will immediately catch the token count discrepancy once multiple days elapse.

tips_feedback.tip: Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer.
tips_feedback.why: Town heavily considered whether Heidi was an honest Roleplayer receiving false information versus malicious. Heidi forcefully rejecting the Roleplayer theory closed off that escape hatch, cementing the unanimous Guilty verdict needed for the Jester win.

lessons.tip: Before a trial, ask whether the nominee gains from dying. A Jester wins when hanged, and Heidi pushed hard for her own hanging, which drew a unanimous Guilty vote. Jester revenge then killed Ivan, a Guilty voter. Check Jester and Executioner incentives before a unanimous hang, and avoid visible Guilty votes on a suspect who is clearly pushing for death.

Check every claimed role against its mechanical limits. Surveyor has two tokens, so three group results cannot be a literal Surveyor. Judy's claim collapsed on that point. A fake role claim should keep its results within the role's token limits and visit rules, or the table will catch it.

Weight a visit list by when its names were predicted. Grace named Carol, Mallory and Niaj as Alice's visitors before any of them spoke, which is much harder to fake than a list assembled after public claims. Prefer predictions made before the named players commit over lists built from the table's existing claims.

Keep private messages and coordinated scripts minimal. Judy and Mallory's PM cluster and matching Innocent votes made Judy the visible target once Mallory was exposed. Give teammates different wording and avoid triangles that the Village can map.

tips_feedback.tip: Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them.
tips_feedback.why: Dave and Erin used the Judy and Mallory PM cluster and their shared Innocent votes on Bob to build the case that got Judy hanged on Day 5, which ended the game for the Village.

lessons.applies_to: Anyone making a false role claim
lessons.tip: Keep a running ledger of that role’s limits, tokens, visits, and result timing. A claim that exceeds a hard limit—such as using more limited actions than the role allows—can undo an otherwise convincing bluff.

Treat a role drawn from a group as probabilistic evidence, not an identity confirmation. Track which players were eligible and how likely each was to produce the result before using it to clear or accuse someone.

Agree on one concise, final night plan: Katana holder, target, and each member’s separate action. Confirm the settled plan once, then avoid contradictory revisions that create execution errors or leave teammates uncertain.

Separate what a result establishes from what it merely suggests. A visitor list can prove someone visited a target, but not that they attacked; account for all plausible visitors and effects before treating the list as a solved deduction.

Role-blocking a Medic only matters if they are the one protecting the Katana target; check protection claims before spending the block, and coordinate blocks with the Katana attack so both land on the same night.

Avoid long repetitive confirmation loops in Yakuza chat; agree targets once with explicit names and roles, and record each member's Diviner or Surveyor result privately so public claims can be kept consistent.

Do not make false public claims that conflict with your own private knowledge of nights; a fake Medic claim on a visited target gets exposed by a flip, and inconsistent Surveyor reports (more groups than tokens) are easy to catch.

Watch for trials decided by a single contested investigative claim; the town repeatedly hanged its own reads (Heidi, Bob, Judy) on unverified results, so demand a checkable detail and avoid tying your vote to one party's narrative.

Track Katana holder and token counts carefully: a Katana holder who dies passes the Katana, and Jester revenge or Serial Killer attacks can kill players at night, so count deaths and visits when evaluating a Lookout or Tracker claim.

When someone claims a result that cannot be true, first check whether an information role could have seen or deduced it before the claim was made. A result that predicts facts before they become public is strong evidence; a result that merely repeats public claims is weak.

Use your role-blocker and killer together. Role-blocking a likely protector can make a kill land, and framing or forging a will can send the town after the wrong player the next day. Coordinate who blocks, who kills, and whose will gets forged in the same night plan.

Write down exact vote counts and timing. Who voted Guilty before a role was revealed, who joined a wagon late, and who defended a confirmed evil player are often more reliable than emotional reads during the day.

If you are repeatedly role-blocked, treat that as information: someone thinks you are dangerous. Protect confirmed or highly likely Good players, and consider self-protection once evil has reason to kill you.

Don’t make your cover claim too convenient. A fake role that explains one suspicious fact can still collapse later when another confirmed result or flip boxes you in. Stay flexible and avoid overcommitting to a story that requires everyone else to misread the mechanics.

summary: Village won. Niaj's free Standard protection on Alice stopped the Katana on N1, but the Serial Killer (Carol) still killed her. Alice's death turned Executioner Heidi into a Jester. Grace's N1 Lookout report (Bob, Carol, Frank, Mallory, Niaj on Alice) was the backbone of the game. She named Mallory, Niaj and Carol before any of them claimed, which made the list credible and forced every Alice visitor to explain themselves. The Yakuza fake claims all clashed with living Village roles. Bob claimed Sheriff to cover his frame visit, and the real Sheriff Frank checked him (Evil). Mallory claimed Medic against the real Medic Niaj. Judy claimed Surveyor and later gave three results from a two-token role. Heidi, now a Jester, fake-claimed Tracker to contradict Grace. The town hanged her 11-0, so her revenge killed Ivan. Bob, Mallory and Judy voted as a bloc: Guilty on Grace, No/Innocent on Bob. That gave the town a clear link. Bob was hanged D3. Erin's Vigilante shot killed the Katana holder Mallory N3. With Bob, Mallory and Frank flipped, Carol was the only unexplained visitor on Grace's list, and she was hanged D4. Judy's token contradiction and her voting links got her hanged D5. On the Yakuza side, Mallory's Pharmacist block on Niaj on N2 and N3 was effective. But the Yakuza Katana hit the same target as the SK both nights, so they effectively wasted those kills.

lessons.tip: If an Executioner's possible target died at night, an Executioner-turned-Jester may be in play. A lone, uncorroborated claimant who contradicts a well-supported report and seems eager to be tried is a Jester candidate. Don't pile on Guilty. Leave them alive, or at least keep the Guilty votes to the bare majority, because the revenge hits a random Guilty voter.
lessons.evidence: Heidi (Jester, formerly Executioner on Alice) fake-claimed Tracker 'Grace→Dave', nominated Grace, and stuck to her story. The town hanged her 11-0, giving her the win, and her revenge killed Prosecutor Ivan, whose prosecution tokens were never used.

lessons.applies_to: Lookout, Tracker and other visit-based investigators
lessons.tip: Post your full visitor list before the visited players claim. Naming players before they explain their visits is the strongest proof a real watcher has, so point it out explicitly when you are challenged. Then use flips to eliminate names until only the killer is left.
lessons.evidence: Grace named Carol, Mallory and Niaj before they spoke. Dave's timeline correction flipped the Grace trial and the later Heidi trial. On D4, Bob, Mallory and Frank had flipped and Niaj was confirmed Medic by Mallory's Pharmacist flip, so only Carol was left as the SK.

lessons.tip: Never fake a role that a living Village player is likely to hold and counterclaim, and never fake a token role beyond its token limit. If you visited a watched target, a cover like 'Vanilla, no action' isn't available. Pick a claim that has no living counterpart, or one whose results can't be checked.
lessons.evidence: Mallory's Medic claim ran into Niaj's real Medic claim. Bob's Sheriff claim ran into Frank, who checked him and got Evil. Judy claimed Surveyor and reported three results from a two-token role. Her late switch to Roleplayer convinced nobody, and she was hanged D5.

lessons.tip: Don't vote as a block. Once one teammate flips, every shared Guilty or Innocent vote becomes the town's case against the rest. When a teammate's trial is clearly lost, it can be better to vote Guilty with the town.
lessons.evidence: Bob, Judy and Mallory all voted Guilty on the real Lookout Grace and No/Innocent on Bob. After Bob and Mallory flipped, Dave and Erin cited exactly these votes to hang Judy.

lessons.tip: Once the Medic is identified, have your role-blocker block them every night you attack a protected-looking target. Also expect a neutral killer to be hunting the same loud information roles. Spread your attack to a second high-value target so both kills don't land on the same player.
lessons.evidence: Mallory blocked Niaj on N2 and N3, which stopped his Strong protections on Grace and Frank. But Carol's SK attack hit the same target both nights, so the Katana added no extra kills and the Village kept its numbers.

lessons.tip: Shoot the player a confirmed or near-confirmed report places on a victim, especially when that player is one of two people claiming the same role. A Basic shot (1 token) kills most roles, which have no Defense. Save the rest unless you suspect a Neutral with innate Defense.
lessons.evidence: Erin shot Mallory, who was on Grace's list and the duplicate Medic claimant. She was the Pharmacist and the Katana holder. It worked, but Erin spent all 3 tokens on a Strong shot when Basic would have done.

lessons.tip: When two players claim Sheriff and share a result on a player who flipped Good, the shared result confirms neither of them. Break the tie with an independent check of one claimant, and look at who visited the framed player.
lessons.evidence: Bob and Frank both said Alice was Evil. Alice had been framed by Bob, which is also why she read Evil. Frank's N2 check on Bob (Evil) plus Bob's Guilty vote on Grace got Bob hanged, and he flipped Fabricator.

tips_feedback.tip: Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction. Actions are optional, most roles aren't unique...
tips_feedback.why: Dave's ledger check showed Grace had named Carol, Mallory and Niaj before they claimed. That saved the real Lookout and reversed the Ivan/Bob/Carol case built on a misremembered timeline. The tip's 'roles aren't unique' point was also used, by Erin, Frank and Ivan, to dismiss Niaj's correct case against Mallory, so it shows that a bad premise doesn't make the conclusion false.

tips_feedback.tip: Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them...
tips_feedback.why: After Bob and Mallory flipped, Dave and Erin cited Judy's Innocent vote on Bob with Mallory, her Guilty vote on Grace, and the Mallory–Judy PMs to hang the last Yakuza on D5.

tips_feedback.tip: Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer.
tips_feedback.why: Erin caught Judy's three Surveyor results against a two-token limit, a contradiction in Judy's own claim, and explained why the Roleplayer excuse didn't fit. Grace also used the Roleplayer framing to survive her trial.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't hang a power claimant just because the claim came late; ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits.
tips_feedback.why: Ivan and Dave, who had this tip, never asked who benefits when the town hanged lone 'Tracker' Heidi. Both voted Guilty in the 11-0 vote, and a Jester was the beneficiary. Ivan died to her revenge. This tip set needs a Jester and Executioner warning.

tips_feedback.tip: Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, a flipped Yakuza's vote or PM partners...). Use Basic shots and never announce whom you'll shoot.
tips_feedback.why: Erin shot the duplicate Medic claimant, who was also on Grace's visitor list, and killed Mallory, the Pharmacist and Katana holder. She ignored the Basic-shot advice and wasted 2 extra tokens.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them.
tips_feedback.why: Dave and Erin pointed out that the Sheriff sees the SK as Not Evil, so Bob's 'Carol = Evil' result couldn't be an SK catch. That kept the town from treating Carol's Ex-Con claim and Bob's result as settled, and the SK was later found by visitor elimination.

issues.description: Night 1: the program has no op to change a role. When the Executioner's target (Alice) died at night, the moderator flagged that Heidi's conversion to Jester was not applied. Its apply_changes workaround then failed with 'target is set by code at setup and can't be changed; nothing was applied'. Even so, the moderator summary claims it 'set status became_jester'. The code apparently did handle the conversion itself: a code message to Heidi at Day 2, her Jester flip, and the Jester revenge all worked. So the moderator's flag was wrong, and its failed write was reported as a success.
Heidi was told twice that she became a Jester: once by the moderator during Night 1 resolution, and again by a code message at the start of Day 2.

The kill op allows only one 'by' and one cause. Grace was killed by both the Katana (Standard) and the SK (Strong) on Night 2, and the moderator had to improvise the cause 'Katana and Serial Killer'. The R12 public reveal therefore depends on a workaround.

Death causes were reported inconsistently. Grace (Night 2) was shown as 'killed by Katana and Serial Killer'. Frank (Night 3) was also hit by both a successful Katana attack and the SK, but was publicly shown only as 'killed by Serial Killer'. This implies the Katana did not kill him. Mallory was even told her Katana attack on Frank succeeded.

R3/R12 do not say what cause of death is publicly revealed when several attacks that each beat the target's Defense hit the same player. Should it be all causes, one chosen at random, or the strongest? This led to the inconsistent handling of Grace and Frank.

Philanthropist feedback was inconsistent. On Night 2 Dave was told 'You handed Judy a philanthropy token. You have 1 philanthropy token left.' The night check flagged this as against instructions, because code handles give_token notifications. On Night 3 the same gift drew no message to Dave. The wording arguably doesn't reveal whether the token was used, but the inconsistency could leak information.

Niaj (deepseek-v4.1-flash) twice produced unparsable answers because of finish_reason length. The model ran out of output tokens while still reasoning, which suggests the output limit is too small for this model's verbose reasoning. The raw reasoning snippets were also written into the log.

Niaj claimed on Day 2 that 'there is only one Medic' and nominated Mallory on that basis. No rule says this: only the Vulture is unique, and the role list isn't public. Several players corrected it and Niaj later retracted.
On Day 2, Judy argued that Grace's visitor list 'omits the confirmed killer'. In fact the SK was necessarily one of the five listed visitors. She retracted this later the same Day.
Night 4: Judy was told 'Your Diviner result on Erin will be sent to you separately' after that result had already been sent. This is a harmless but confusing ordering/wording artifact.
